@LoriBal34682344 @redpilldispensr Christy, I'm as concerned about Digital ID as anyone, and as everyone should be. Please don't misunderstand what I'm about to say.

However, let me offer an opinion on Costco. The whole membership idea, particularly with your photo on the Costco membership card — actually started as a way to limit shoplifting — and to elevate the shopping experience.

People planning to shoplift really don't want to hand over their driver's license and get their picture taken. In fact, there is a whole level of society, a lower level, that doesn't like this idea.

Ever wonder why the shopping experience at Costco is so pleasant? It's because those people aren't there.

The membership fee adds to this, although there are other marketing reasons for the fee. (People are more likely to shop at a place when they've already paid a fee to shop there.)

Having the card scanned is likely just an anti-counterfeit thing. It's easy to make a fake Costco card these days, but if it needs a registered serial number in that bar code, it takes a scan to find out.

The problem with Digital ID is not so much the details of how it works, but the intent behind it. Costco wants to run a nice business. The government wants to control your life.

@DhalsimDo73431 @Felippe_Hermes Vamos detalhar os dois casos: supermercados tradicionais vs. Costco.

**Supermercados tradicionais:**
- Lucram com margens altas nos produtos (25-50%). Para maximizar, fazem acordos com marcas: pagam por espaço na prateleira (slotting fees) ou promoções. Isso pode priorizar produtos caros/populares, não os melhores/baratos. Ex: Uma marca de cereal paga para ficar no olho do cliente, mesmo se houver opção mais barata.

**Costco:**
- Lucro principal das taxas anuais (US$60-120, ~70% do lucro). Margens nos produtos são baixas (10-15%). Sem depender de margens altas, negociam preços diretos e baixos com fornecedores, sem acordos pagos. Priorizam o melhor valor. Ex: Vodka Kirkland (marca própria) usa fornecedor premium, vendida barata, sem propaganda de marca.

与优衣库相反的是，MUJI 的品牌源头就是汉字「無印良品」。但入华的时候，「无印良品」四个中文字的商标已经被抢注了，无奈只能转而塑造 MUJI 商标。

不过后来，因为 iPhone 的成功，「使用统一的罗马字品牌」成了新的黄金标准。Nike、IKEA、Costco、Tesla、Lego……连宝马这么神的意译，都用回了 BMW。

包括中国企业出海的过程中，也能看到这件事的重要性：品牌的罗马字需要符合主流的「发音习惯」，更容易形成传播。做到这一点的如 Nio、Anker、TikTok……典型的反面例子则毫无疑问是 Xiaomi 和 Huawei。

@PecanC8 @oX_Bat_Xo Many  items  in the US are manufactured in Canadian: widely available at retailers like Costco, Walmart…

- **Halls Cough Drops**: Produced in a Scarborough, Ontario factory, which makes over 6 billion pieces annually for distribution across North America.
- **Swedish Fish and Sour Patch Kids**: All North American production occurs in Hamilton, Ontario, supplying billions of pieces yearly to US stores.
- **Kirkland Signature Products** (Costco's private label): Many items, like certain cheeses, nuts, and baked goods, are sourced and produced in Canada for US sales.
- **Tim Hortons Coffee and Baked Goods**: Roasted and packaged in Canada using original recipes; available at US locations and in grocery aisles.
- **Voortman and Leclerc Cookies**: Baked in Canadian facilities and stocked in US supermarkets for popular varieties like wafers and shortbread.
- **Maple Syrup**: Quebec produces over 70% of the world's supply, with major exports to the US for brands like those sold at Trader Joe's and Whole Foods.
- **Peace by Chocolate Bars**: Handmade in Nova Scotia
- **Clark's Baked Beans**: Canned in Ontario since 1877
- **Crown Royal Whisky**: Distilled and aged entirely in Canada; the top-selling Canadian whisky in the US, with over 7 million cases annually.
- **Canadian Beers** (e.g., Molson, Labatt): Brewed in Canada and imported to the US for brands like Budweiser variants produced..

Snacks
Canada's candy industry supplies a surprising amount of US favorites:

- **Maynards Candy** (including US-distributed lines): Made in Ontario 
- **Dino Nuggets**: Produced in Canada and sold at US Costcos as a kid-friendly frozen snack.

These brands leverage Canadian manufacturing:
- **MAC Cosmetics**: Founded in Toronto; many products are still manufactured in Canada and sold at US Sephora.
- **Snuggles Fabric Softener**: Labeled as Canadian-made and available in US 
- **French's Ketchup**: Uses 100% Canadian-grown tomatoes; bottled in Canada for US markets.

Canadian fashion in US wardrobes:

- **Aritzia Clothing**: Vancouver-based designs manufactured in Canada; stores across the US carry lines like blazers and activewear.
- **Tilley Hats**: Iconic waterproof hats made in Canada; sold at US outdoor retailers with lifetime guarantees.
- **Herschel Supply Backpacks and Bags**: Produced in Canada; popular at US Targets and Urban Outfitters.
- **Roots Apparel**: Toronto-founded; select leather goods and casual wear still made in Canada, available at US outlets.

Gear:
- **Sabian Cymbals**: Crafted in New Brunswick; used by US musicians like those in Rush and the Black Eyed Peas, sold at music stores nationwide.
- **Sam Bat Baseball Bats**: Maple wood bats from Ontario; over 100 MLB players used them in recent seasons, available at sporting goods shops.
- **Cervélo Bikes**: High-performance models built in Toronto; favored by US cyclists for speed and lightness.
- **Napoleon Grills**: Barrie, Ontario-made BBQs; North America's largest privately owned brand, sold at US Home Depot locations.

Vehicles and Automotive Parts
Under the USMCA, many cars assembled in Canada are sold in the US.

- **Honda Civic and CR-V**: Built in Alliston, Ontario; popular sedans and SUVs in US showrooms.
- **Toyota RAV4**: Assembled in Cambridge, Ontario; one of the best-selling vehicles in the US.
- **Ford Edge and Lincoln Nautilus**: Produced in Oakville, Ontario; mid-size SUVs for US families.
- **Chrysler Pacifica Minivan**: Made in Windsor, Ontario; a top family hauler in the US market.

Other Notables
- **Lumber and Wood Products**: Canada supplies over 25% of US softwood lumber for construction, essential for housing.
- **Aluminum**: Raw aluminum from Quebec smelters used in US cans, cars, and aircraft.
- **Potatoes**: Canadian varieties feed into US processed foods like fries at McDonald's.

These products highlight the deep integration of the North American supply chains, with Canada exporting over $400 billion in goods to the US annually.

Working at Costco was one of the worst experiences of my professional life. What’s marketed as a great retailer with solid benefits and a positive culture is, in reality, a breeding ground for bullying and mistreatment. From day one, I witnessed and experienced a toxic environment where harassment and discrimination run rampant, especially toward vulnerable groups like autistic individuals and women.

The bullying is systemic. Managers and coworkers often target anyone who doesn't fit the mold, creating a hostile atmosphere where complaints are dismissed or turned against the victim. Autistic employees, in particular, face unfair treatment—whether it's ignoring requests for accommodations or outright harassment based on disabilities

Women aren't spared either; I've seen gender-based discrimination, including unequal handling of issues and a culture that overlooks harassment.

It's not just isolated incidents—there are multiple reports and legal cases highlighting racism, unfair terminations, and failure to address complaints properly.

What’s even more infuriating is how the company handles investigations. They seem to spend more time scrutinizing minor or unrelated issues—like probing into flagged reports or policies—than actually protecting vulnerable employees from real harm.

Confidentiality rules during probes often silence workers, violating labor rights and leaving abusers unchecked.

Instead of fostering safety, leadership focuses on covering their tracks, which only emboldens the bullies.If you can't take the abuse, you're out. Costco has a pattern of firing those who speak up or refuse to endure the mistreatment, often under the guise of policy violations.

It's not a place for growth or support—it's survival of the fittest, where the company protects its image over its people. Avoid at all costs if you're looking for a respectful workplace.

Deep beneath the blandest strip mall in Provo, Utah—between a Panda Express and a mattress outlet—lurks the Dark Dungeon Lair of Khaki Costco Love, headquarters of the Khlysty Darksect Army. Their leader, Hal Atkin, arrives precisely at 6:00 p.m., punctual as always, armed with a clipboard, a coupon book, and a burning desire to “awaken the sleeping spirits of bulk purchasing power.”

Around him, the other Darksect “initiates” shuffle awkwardly in their black robes—except under those robes? Khakis. Always khakis. A faint scent of rotisserie chicken fills the air. The candles are vanilla-scented. Their sacred altar? A refurbished Costco display table labeled “Seasonal Deals.”

A hush falls. Someone turns down the Enya Meets Black Sabbath playlist.

The fluorescent lights flicker. A soft hum fills the room. For a moment, they believe they’ve breached dimensions—until Hal realizes he accidentally sat on the TV remote.

Still, in that surreal moment, surrounded by bulk mayonnaise, LED candles, and $15 fleece blankets, the Khlysty Darksect feels powerful. Unified. Deeply ridiculous.

During everything.

Dealer takedown is the safety valve in the auction process. They’re the middle men who move goods from the supplier (the debt issuer) to the consumer (the debt’s final balance sheet owner). Think of them as the discount wholesaler (Costco) of the bond market. By definition they will have the worst bid for the goods because they need to make a wholesaling profit. They don’t want to own the risk of the goods inside the shipping container (hold debt on balance sheet like a bank, insurance company, etc). They are in the business of shipping container throughput.

Higher dealer takedown = deeper concession on the auction that tends to come with a significant tail; it’s a good sign rates will want to come in short term over the life of the current OTR as dealers place the issue to their client accounts profitably. 

Yesterday we saw low dealer takedown = dealers didn’t need to come in to support the auction, because demand from other financial institutions picked it up. And this was in a week that saw some major geopolitical realignments (Argentina) and reaffirmations (Japan) that will likely stand out as significant developments in our multi-century big picture civilizational narrative. Yields might drift higher in the short term but this isn’t the end of the world “dealers are giving up on this @USTreasury Department” you’re seeing from doomposters.

Kitten's Story for Kam 
Story Two~Part One

Title: Kam and the Hidden 63rd

Nobody knew exactly when Kam decided he was an explorer. One day he was just Kam, snack enthusiast, chaotic driver, man who once got lost in a Costco for an hour, and the next, he had a safari hat, an old Polaroid camera, and a wrinkled napkin from a Seattle coffee shop he called The Map of Destiny.

He laid it out on Kitten’s kitchen table like it was the Rosetta Stone.

“This,” Kam declared, jabbing a finger dramatically at a particularly aggressive coffee stain, “is the key to finding the hidden 63rd National Park that the government doesn’t want us to know about.”

Kitten raised an eyebrow. “Kam, that’s a latte stain shaped like Florida.”

“Exactly!” Kam said, eyes wide with the kind of confidence only found in late-night YouTube documentaries. “The Florida-shaped stain points to the truth. The government added an extra national park but hid it after ‘The Great Map Scandal of 1983.’”

AV peeked over the table, swirling his iced espresso like a detective. “You’re basing this on… a spill?”

“Not just any spill.” Kam said. “A prophetic one. The steam from my mocha spoke to me.”

Doom, who had been sitting silently in the corner, adjusting his gloves and muttering something about “entropy,” finally said, “I once saw a face in my toast.”

Markus, leaning against the fridge, sighed. “Kam, even your compass points at Chipotle.”

Kam straightened his hat. “Gentlemen. Kitten. At dawn, we become unauthorized explorers.”

Kitten stared. “You mean criminals?”

“Adventurers.” Kam corrected, stuffing the map into his pocket like Indiana Jones with ADHD.

Scene 1: Departure from Sanity

The next morning, Kam’s van, a dented, sticker-covered beast named The Blunderbus, rumbled to life in a puff of smoke and mystery.

The dashboard was covered in Post-it notes labeled things like “Possible Vortex Site?”, “Government Beaver Dams?”, and one that simply read “Snacks.”

Kam wore aviators and a bomber jacket despite it being 83 degrees. “Team, this is it. Today, we uncover the truth hidden between Yosemite and Wi-Fi dead zones.”

Kitten climbed into the passenger seat with a sigh. “Your GPS says we’re heading toward ‘Unidentified Cow Fields.’”

Kam pointed proudly to the glove compartment. “Who needs GPS when you’ve got destiny and gas station trail mix?”

Thirty miles later, they were hopelessly lost.

“Kam.” AV said, “The road ended twenty minutes ago.”

“Nature is the road.” Kam replied, driving straight into a patch of sagebrush.

Doom adjusted his shades. “If we die out here, I’m haunting the Park Service.”

Scene 2: The Gas Station Oracle

They stopped at a lonely desert gas station called Bob’s Fuel & Bait, population: Bob, two tumbleweeds, and an ancient Coca-Cola sign that creaked like a prophecy.

Inside, Kam questioned the attendant. “You ever heard of a hidden national park? One that doesn’t exist on any map?”

Bob blinked. “You mean the one that disappears when you look at it?”

Kam’s jaw dropped. “YES!”

Bob shrugged. “Or maybe that was my ex-wife’s house. Hard to tell.”

Kam gasped anyway and bought a suspiciously overpriced compass, an inflatable kayak, and a can labeled ‘Emergency Beans.’

When he returned to the van, Kitten said, “Please tell me you didn’t just spend $80 on beans.”

“They’re government beans, Kitten.”

Scene 3: The Desert of Dubious Discoveries

They set up camp in the desert under an arch of red sandstone. Kam stood with his foot on a cooler, gazing heroically into the horizon.

“This is it.” he said. “We’re standing on the very soil of the 63rd Park.”

Costco vient de dépasser les $250 milliards de revenus annuels.

Et leur modèle économique est tellement simple que ça en devient génial.

Ils vendent tout presque sans marge. Les produits sont vendus avec 10-15% de markup maximum. Parfois moins. Walmart fait 25%, Target 30%. Costco refuse de monter au-dessus de 15%.

Alors comment ils gagnent de l'argent ?

Les frais d'adhésion. $65 par an pour être membre. Ils ont 130 millions de membres dans le monde. Fais le calcul : $8.5 milliards de revenus purs. Sans vendre un seul produit.

Et voici le truc brillant : ce revenu arrive avant même que tu achètes quoi que ce soit. C'est du cash garanti, prévisible, récurrent. Les investisseurs adorent la prévisibilité.

Le taux de renouvellement est à 93%. Une fois que t'es membre, tu restes membre. Parce que les prix sont tellement bas que tu rentabilises ton abonnement en 2-3 visites.

Pendant que Amazon se bat sur la livraison rapide et les algorithmes complexes, Costco fait l'inverse. Des entrepôts géants, pas de décoration, des palettes au sol, et des prix imbattables.

Ils vendent seulement 4,000 produits. Amazon en a 350 millions. Mais Costco négocie des volumes massifs sur ces 4,000 références et obtient des prix que personne d'autre ne peut avoir.

Le business model n'a pas changé depuis 40 ans. Pas de disruption technologique. Pas de révolution digitale. Juste une exécution parfaite d'un concept ultra simple.

Pendant que tout le monde parle de tech, d'IA et d'innovation, Costco prouve qu'un modèle basique bien exécuté écrase la complexité.

Parfois, le plus simple gagne.

Morning Costco run to replenish supplies.

Water, coffee, toilet paper, snacks and freezer & fridge full of food. Even a big screen projector TV.
